title: Al-Khwarizmi: The Father of Algebra
summary: How the Baghdad scholar Al-Khwarizmi wrote step-by-step methods that gave us algebra, spread the numbers we use today, and lent his name to the word algorithm.
poll: Ideas from long ago still matter in our lives today.

versions.title: The Man Who Gave Us Algebra
versions.text:
Do you like math? Then thank a man from long ago. His name was Al-Khwarizmi.

He was born a long, long time ago. He grew up in Central Asia. Then he went to a big city. It was Baghdad.

Baghdad had a great place to learn. It was the House of Wisdom. It was full of books. Wise men came there. They read. They wrote. Each one was a scholar. He was one of them.

He wrote a book on math. It showed how to find a lost number. It gave steps to solve each sum. Do one step. Then do the next. Folks used his steps to share land. They used them to buy and sell, too. A word in his book gave us the name algebra.

He wrote on numbers, too. He used ten signs. They came from India. One sign was zero. We still use these signs. His books went to Europe. The new way spread.

His name gave us a word, too. That word is algorithm. It means a list of steps. A computer runs on steps like that. So think of him when you do math!

versions.title: Al-Khwarizmi: The Father of Algebra
versions.text:
Do you like solving math problems? If you do, you can thank a scholar who lived more than twelve hundred years ago. His name was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. He is often called the father of algebra.

He was born around the year 780 in a part of Central Asia. As a young man, he moved to Baghdad. At that time, it was one of the largest cities in the world.

Baghdad had a famous place of learning called the House of Wisdom. Its library held books from Greece, Persia, India, and other lands. Scholars worked to translate these books into Arabic. They also studied math, the stars, and maps. Al-Khwarizmi became one of its most important thinkers.

His most famous book showed how to solve an equation. An equation is a math sentence with a missing number. He gave clear steps for each type of problem. One key idea was to keep both sides of the equation in balance. People used his methods to share land fairly and to buy and sell goods. One word in the title of his book was al-jabr, and that word gave us the name algebra.

He also wrote a book about the number system from India. It used just ten signs, and one of them was zero. The place of each sign showed how much it was worth. These are the numbers we use today. Later, his books were translated into Latin, and the new numbers spread across Europe.

Even his name became a word. In Europe, people wrote his name as Algoritmi. Today we say algorithm, which means a set of steps for solving a problem. Every computer follows algorithms, so his ideas are still at work all around us.

Individuals who derive genuine satisfaction from resolving intricate mathematical problems owe a considerable intellectual debt to a scholar who flourished more than twelve centuries ago, a man named Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, who is frequently and quite justly described as the father of algebra as a formal discipline.

Al-Khwarizmi was born around the year 780 within Khwarazm, a region situated within Central Asia that ultimately bestowed upon him his enduring and now-famous name. As a young man, he relocated to Baghdad, which constituted, during that particular era, one of the largest, wealthiest, and most intellectually vibrant metropolises found anywhere within the civilized world.

Baghdad was home to a celebrated institution of advanced scholarship known as the House of Wisdom. Its extensive library housed countless manuscripts originating from Greece, Persia, India, and numerous other distant civilizations, and the resident scholars labored diligently and continuously to translate these foreign texts into Arabic while simultaneously investigating disciplines such as mathematics, astronomy, and geography with considerable rigor. Al-Khwarizmi emerged as one of its most influential and widely respected intellectuals, and he additionally compiled exhaustive astronomical tables that enabled practicing astronomers to calculate, with impressive precision, the movements of the sun, moon, and planets, alongside a comprehensive geographical treatise that meticulously recorded the precise locations of innumerable cities across the known world.

His most celebrated and enduring treatise explained methodically how to solve an equation, a mathematical statement containing some unknown quantity requiring careful determination. Rather than merely offering a scattered, haphazard assortment of unrelated tricks, he presented a rigorously systematic method applicable to each distinct category of problem, meticulously describing every procedure through a sequence of careful, logically ordered stages. One essential underlying principle required maintaining both sides of an equation in perfect, unwavering balance, so that whatever operation one performed upon one side, one performed identically upon the other. Merchants, land surveyors, and government officials subsequently applied his methods extensively to divide land equitably and to calculate commercial prices with newfound mathematical confidence. One particularly significant word appearing within the title of his treatise was al-jabr, signifying "restoring" or "completion," and that very word eventually furnished us with the modern mathematical term algebra.

Al-Khwarizmi additionally composed a separate treatise describing the numerical system that originated within India, a system that employed merely ten distinct numerals, including the crucial numeral zero, and within which the positional placement of each numeral determined its overall mathematical value. These numerals remain essentially identical to those we continue employing in arithmetic today, and centuries afterward, his treatises were translated meticulously into Latin, whereupon these innovative numerals gradually disseminated throughout medieval Europe, eventually supplanting older, considerably more cumbersome systems such as Roman numerals in virtually every practical application.

Remarkably, even his own personal name eventually became a word in common scientific usage, since European writers transliterated his name as Algoritmi, and today we consequently employ the resulting term algorithm, signifying a precise, carefully ordered sequence of instructions designed methodically to solve a particular class of problem. Greek
Persian
Latin
questions.why: The article says his books were translated into Latin, and the new numbers spread across Europe.

wrong.A: Scholars in Baghdad translated other books into Arabic.
wrong.B: Greek books came to Baghdad; his books were not translated into Greek.
wrong.C: Persian books came to the library, but the article does not say his books were put into Persian.

questions.stem: Read: "keep both sides of the equation in balance." What does balance mean here?
options: Moving quickly
Equal on both sides
Written in Arabic
Larger on one side
questions.why: Keeping the sides in balance means whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, so they stay equal.

wrong.C: The language is not what balance means.
wrong.D: This is the opposite of balance.

questions.stem: What caused the new numbers to spread across Europe?
options: Computers carried them there.
His books were translated into Latin.
Roman soldiers brought them from India.
Scholars in Europe invented them.
questions.why: The article says that after his books were translated into Latin, the new numbers spread across Europe.

wrong.C: The article does not say this.
wrong.D: The numbers came from India, not Europe.

questions.stem: Why did scholars at the House of Wisdom translate books into Arabic?
options: To keep the books secret
To sell the books to people living far away in Europe
So they could learn ideas from other lands
Because the old books were too short
questions.why: The books came from Greece, Persia, and India, so translating them let Baghdad's scholars read and build on those ideas.

wrong.A: Translating makes books easier to share, not secret.
wrong.B: The article does not say the books were sold in Europe.
wrong.D: Length has nothing to do with translation.

questions.stem: In this number system, the place of each sign shows its value. What can you infer about the numbers 52 and 25?
options: They are the same amount.
They both mean zero.
They cannot be written using only the ten signs from India.
They show different amounts.
questions.why: The 5 and 2 are in different places in each number, so their values change.

wrong.A: Place changes the value, so they are different.
wrong.C: Both use the signs 5 and 2, which are part of the ten signs.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with algorithms and computers?
options: To show that his ideas still matter today
To explain how to fix a computer
To prove that he lived in modern times
To compare Baghdad and Europe
questions.why: Ending with computers shows readers that a scholar from long ago still affects their lives.

wrong.B: The article gives no computer repair steps.
wrong.C: He lived more than twelve hundred years ago.
wrong.D: The ending is about his name and computers, not cities.

MID.prompt: Explain why Al-Khwarizmi is called the father of algebra. Use at least three details from the article in your answer.
checklist: I explained what Al-Khwarizmi did in his famous book.
I used at least three details from the article.
I connected the details to the title "father of algebra."
MID.modelAnswer: Al-Khwarizmi is called the father of algebra because he wrote a famous book that explained clear steps for solving an equation, a math sentence with a missing number. One key idea in his book was to keep both sides of the equation in balance, so whatever you did to one side, you had to do to the other. The word al-jabr from the title of his book was later translated into Latin and changed into the word algebra, which is why people still call him its father today.

keyWords.definition: done by following a careful, organized plan
keyWords.example: She took a systematic approach and checked every shelf in order.

keyWords.definition: a written sign that stands for a number
keyWords.example: The clock on the tower used Roman numerals instead of regular numbers.

keyWords.definition: having a strong effect on people or ideas
keyWords.example: The influential teacher inspired many students to become scientists.

keyWords.definition: the science of stars, planets, and space
keyWords.example: His interest in astronomy began when he saw Saturn through a telescope.

keyWords.definition: a book or paper written by hand
keyWords.example: The museum kept the old manuscript behind glass to protect it.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: His systematic work shaped algebra, numerals, and algorithms.
The House of Wisdom was the largest library ever built.
European scholars invented most of modern mathematics without help from others.
Astronomy was more important than mathematics in Baghdad.
questions.why: The article shows how his methods, his book on numerals, and even his name influenced mathematics and computing.

wrong.B: The article does not make this claim.
wrong.C: The article shows that key ideas reached Europe through his books.
wrong.D: The article does not rank these subjects.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does the word al-jabr mean?
options: Counting
Balancing
Restoring
Dividing
questions.why: The article states that al-jabr means "restoring."

wrong.A: This is not the meaning given.
wrong.B: Balance is a principle he used, but the article says al-jabr means restoring.
wrong.D: Dividing land was one use of his methods, not the word's meaning.

questions.stem: Where did Al-Khwarizmi's name come from?
options: The House of Wisdom
Khwarazm, a region
A Latin word for numbers
The title of the famous book he wrote in Baghdad
questions.why: The article says he was born in Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia that gave him his name.

wrong.C: Latin writers changed his name; they did not create it.
wrong.D: His book gave us the word algebra, not his name.

questions.stem: Read: "he presented a systematic method for each category of problem." What does systematic mean?
options: Quick and careless
Secret and hidden
Borrowed from another culture
Organized and following a clear plan
questions.why: The article contrasts his method with "scattered tricks," so systematic means organized and planned.

wrong.A: A systematic method is careful, not careless.
wrong.B: He shared his methods in a book.
wrong.C: Systematic describes how the method is organized, not where it came from.

questions.stem: Why do we use the word algorithm today?
options: It was the name of a counting machine built in Baghdad.
It is the Arabic word for computer.
Europeans spelled his name Algoritmi.
It was the title of his book on numerals.
questions.why: The article explains that the European spelling of his name, Algoritmi, became the word algorithm.

wrong.A: The article does not mention such a machine.
wrong.B: The word comes from his name, not a word for computer.
wrong.D: The word came from his name, not a book title.

questions.stem: The library held manuscripts from Greece, Persia, India, and other civilizations. What does this suggest?
options: Baghdad's scholars refused to read foreign books.
Its scholars learned from many cultures.
Only Greek ideas were valued in Baghdad.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote all of the manuscripts in the library himself.
questions.why: Collecting and translating texts from many civilizations shows that scholars learned from and combined many traditions.

wrong.A: They translated foreign books, so they clearly read them.
wrong.C: Books came from many lands, not only Greece.
wrong.D: The manuscripts came from other civilizations.

questions.stem: Why would a systematic method be more useful than a collection of scattered tricks?
options: It worked for any problem of that type.
It made problems more difficult.
It worked only for astronomers studying the planets.
It required a computer.
questions.why: A method for each category of problem lets people solve new problems of that kind, not only special cases.

wrong.B: His methods made problems easier to solve.
wrong.C: People used his methods to divide land and calculate prices, not only astronomers.
wrong.D: Computers did not exist in his time.

questions.stem: How does the paragraph about his most celebrated book develop its ideas?
options: It tells a story about his childhood.
It compares Baghdad with Europe.
It lists the planets he studied.
It describes his method, its practical uses, and then the origin of the word algebra.
questions.why: The paragraph explains equations and balance, shows how people used the methods, and ends with how al-jabr became algebra.

wrong.B: No such comparison is made in that paragraph.
wrong.C: Planets are mentioned in a different paragraph.

HIGH.prompt: The article claims that Al-Khwarizmi's ideas "continue to operate all around us." Write an argument that supports or challenges this claim, using evidence about algebra, numerals, and algorithms from the article.
checklist: I clearly stated whether I support or challenge the claim.
I used specific evidence about at least two of his contributions.
I explained how each piece of evidence connects to life today, with a clear conclusion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I support the claim that Al-Khwarizmi's ideas continue to operate all around us, because his contributions to algebra, numerals, and algorithms remain central to modern life. His systematic, step-by-step method for solving an equation became the foundation of algebra, a subject still taught in classrooms worldwide. He also wrote about the Indian number system, whose ten numerals, including zero, now form the basis of nearly every number written today. Finally, his own name, changed into the word algorithm, describes the instructions every computer follows, from phone apps to search engines. Since algebra, numerals, and algorithms are each so influential in daily life, this one scholar's ideas truly do operate all around us.
